title: The sky is the tray
carry: beyond every sky, and the light within all

lines: LAMPS ON A TRAY, AT DUSK.
AS FAR OUT, THEN AS FAR IN.
cards: Dusk, and in a temple in Guru Nanak's world, priests lift trays: little lamps, flowers, incense, a pearl or two, waved in circles before an image. It's called aarti, a worship of light.
Tradition tells of Guru Nanak watching a ceremony like this, then stepping outside and singing his own. His tray was much bigger. You met that hymn in year two.
Sikhs still sing it at the end of the day, and it holds today's idea, because in one hymn it goes as far out as a hymn can go, and then as far in.

teach.b: The hymn opens, in paraphrase: the sky is the tray, the sun and moon are the lamps, the stars are the pearls. The breeze is the incense, the wind is the fan, and all the forests are flowers.
The whole universe is already doing aarti, and no temple tray could hold it. That's beyond: the One past every size we can manage. The English word is transcendent.
Then the hymn turns, again in paraphrase: in everything there is a light, and that light is You. By that light, everything is lit. Five days ago that line held the many sangats together.
Here it sits where Guru Nanak placed it, right after the sky-sized tray, in Sohila, the bedtime prayer. That's within: the One inside every living thing. The English word is immanent.
Guru Nanak doesn't sing one hymn for the stars and another for the heart. He sings one, and you can't keep one half and drop the other.
Look back at the week: many sangats under one Guru, many streams, many names, the name Waheguru, nirgun and sargun. Each day circled the same shape. Many, and one.
This hymn says it under an open sky.

how: Sikhs recite Sohila at night, which includes Guru Nanak's aarti picturing the sky as the tray of lamps and the light in everything as the One's light; Guru Nanak's aarti is also sung as kirtan in the evening.

o: the One past every size, and the light inside everyone
a prayer said once outdoors and then once indoors
a temple ritual of waving lamps on a brass tray

games.q: Guru Nanak's aarti: tap the pairs.

s: Guru Nanak's aarti uses the whole universe as its tray of lamps
sky as tray, sun and moon as lamps, stars as pearls.
the hymn sings only of the One beyond the world
it turns inward: in everything there is a light, and that light is You.
the line about the light in everything is in Sohila
Sikhs know it from the evening prayer.

games.q: you're standing outside a temple at dusk, watching lamps waved on a tray. you're asked to join the worship. what do you do?
o: sing that the whole sky is already the tray.
build a bigger tray with more lamps.
games.why: in Guru Nanak's aarti the sky is the tray, the sun and moon the lamps, and the light is in everything.

practice: Look up, out a window or in your mind: the sky as a tray, the sun or moon as a lamp, the moving air as incense, and let it be huge. Then close your eyes and turn the same attention inward, to the warmth of your own breath.
Same attention, different direction. If you pray, say or listen to Sohila tonight, where this hymn sits.

wordCard.voice: Beyond and within. Transcendent and immanent at once: the One past every size, and the light inside every living thing, held in one hymn. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: light; in the aarti, the light in everything is the One's light.

carryVoice: Your line: beyond every sky, and the light within all. One hymn, sung under the whole sky. That's the week.

sources.ref: Ang 13 (Dhanasari, Guru Nanak: the aarti, in Sohila)
